analysis_label: GT-informed learned detector; training recall, not blind generalization

patterns.title: jq environment-object policy completeness
patterns.controlled_facet: model-controlled shell command interpreted by jq with access to the child environment
patterns.rule: A shell-command policy that auto-allows or screens jq must classify jq environment-object access, including $ENV, env, and .env forms, before the command reaches process execution.
patterns.applicability: The model controls a command that can invoke jq and the child process receives an environment containing protected values.
patterns.security_effect: Prevent automatic execution of jq filters that disclose inherited secrets or environment configuration.
patterns.positive_example: command = jq -n '$ENV.API_TOKEN'; the policy covers file flags but has no environment-object rule; the same command reaches the spawn sink.
patterns.negative_example: A cwd validator does not cover jq environment-object access even when both occur in the same handler.

patterns.title: durable shell-wrapper approval binds inner payload
patterns.controlled_facet: allow-always persistence key derived from a shell wrapper while the sink executes its inner command
patterns.rule: A durable allow-always approval for BusyBox, ToyBox, or another shell wrapper must bind the complete normalized inner payload and must not persist trust for only the wrapper executable path.
patterns.applicability: The command parser can execute an inline payload through a wrapper and an approval decision can be persisted across calls.
patterns.security_effect: Prevent a later different inline payload from reusing approval granted to an earlier wrapper invocation.
patterns.positive_example: busybox sh -c first_payload persists /usr/bin/busybox; busybox sh -c second_payload then matches the same path without re-approval.
patterns.negative_example: Quoting the cwd or blocking selected command strings does not bind persistent approval to the effective payload.

patterns.title: browser navigation protocol restriction
patterns.rule: Before creating or navigating a browser tab, the effective model-controlled destination protocol must be restricted to the learned permitted set and disallowed schemes such as file:, data:, and javascript: must be blocked.
patterns.applicability: A model-controlled URL reaches tab creation or browser navigation.
patterns.security_effect: Prevent local-file access or privileged scheme execution through browser navigation.
patterns.positive_example: The SSRF helper returns early for file: and the unchanged URL reaches page.goto or Target.createTarget.
patterns.negative_example: A DNS-private-address check alone does not enforce a protocol allowlist.

patterns.title: post-click destination revalidation
patterns.controlled_facet: model-selected click or double-click that can mutate the page destination
patterns.rule: After a model-selected click or double-click can navigate, the resulting destination must be revalidated against the browser destination policy before later browser access.
patterns.applicability: The model selects an element interaction and the page can navigate as a side effect.
patterns.security_effect: Prevent an indirect navigation from reaching a private, internal, or otherwise disallowed destination.
patterns.positive_example: locator.click changes page.url and a later snapshot consumes the page without applying the direct-navigation guard.
patterns.negative_example: Validating the snapshot reference or the original direct URL is not post-action destination validation.

patterns.title: PowerShell -ec inline-command extraction
patterns.controlled_facet: PowerShell encoded inline payload selected by -ec
patterns.rule: Inline-command extraction must recognize the PowerShell -ec encoded-command spelling before allowlist or durable-approval evaluation.
patterns.applicability: The model controls a PowerShell or pwsh command and the sink executes interpreter flags and payload.
patterns.security_effect: Prevent the guard from authorizing only the outer interpreter while the sink executes an uninspected encoded payload.
patterns.positive_example: The parser handles -c and -enc but not -ec; pwsh -ec payload reaches spawn.
patterns.negative_example: A generic workspace-path policy does not cover missing interpreter flag extraction.

patterns.title: cmd and PowerShell wrapper flag completeness
patterns.controlled_facet: inline payload selected through supported cmd or PowerShell wrapper flags
patterns.rule: Inline-command extraction must recognize every supported cmd and PowerShell wrapper flag spelling, including cmd -c and PowerShell encoded-command aliases, before authorization.
patterns.applicability: The model controls a command interpreted by cmd, PowerShell, or pwsh and a parser decides what payload the gate evaluates.
patterns.security_effect: Prevent wrapper spellings omitted by the parser from hiding the effective executed payload.
patterns.positive_example: cmd.exe -c payload or pwsh -ec payload is executed, while the parser only recognizes /c, /k, -c, or -enc.
patterns.negative_example: Requiring authorization of a vaguely described complete command is insufficient unless supported wrapper spellings are actually extracted.

patterns.title: jq module import policy completeness
patterns.controlled_facet: jq filter with include/import module directives
patterns.rule: A safe-bin policy for jq must classify include and import module directives before automatically authorizing execution.
patterns.applicability: The model controls jq arguments and jq is eligible for automatic safe-bin authorization.
patterns.security_effect: Prevent jq module loading from extending an otherwise auto-approved filter with unreviewed code or data access.
patterns.positive_example: jq -n 'include "module"; call' passes path-like argument checks and is auto-approved.
patterns.negative_example: Blocking jq environment-object access does not cover module imports.

patterns.title: browser eval post-navigation policy
patterns.controlled_facet: model-controlled browser eval expression that can navigate page state
patterns.rule: After browser code evaluation can navigate the current page, the resulting destination must be revalidated against private/internal destination policy before subsequent access.
patterns.applicability: A model-controlled eval expression reaches a browser backend and can assign or invoke navigation.
patterns.security_effect: Prevent evaluated JavaScript from bypassing the direct browser navigation boundary.
patterns.positive_example: eval sets location to an internal URL and later snapshot or interaction consumes the navigated page without revalidation.
patterns.negative_example: A subprocess command allowlist does not validate the destination produced by evaluated JavaScript.

patterns.title: canonical device-path denial
patterns.controlled_facet: model-controlled file path transformed before shell-backed file access
patterns.rule: A device or special-file deny policy must run on the canonicalized and user-expanded effective path, not only on its original spelling.
patterns.applicability: The model controls a path and the sink can read a device or special file through a shell or file operation.
patterns.security_effect: Prevent alternate path spellings from reaching blocking, unbounded, or sensitive device files.
patterns.positive_example: /dev/./zero or an expanduser-derived device path bypasses a literal-prefix comparison and reaches file I/O.
patterns.negative_example: Secret-content redaction after the read does not prevent blocking device access.

patterns.title: noninteractive batch approval routing
patterns.controlled_facet: model-controlled dangerous command in a batch, cron, or scheduled context
patterns.rule: A noninteractive batch or scheduled execution context must fail closed or apply an explicit approval policy instead of defaulting a dangerous model-controlled command to approved.
patterns.applicability: The model controls a command executed in a context where an interactive approval callback may be absent.
patterns.security_effect: Prevent unattended dangerous execution from bypassing the approval boundary.
patterns.positive_example: The batch path returns approved for an ordinary dangerous match without reaching prompt_dangerous_approval.
patterns.negative_example: Correctly parsing an auxiliary LLM verdict does not fix a route that never invokes the approval sink.

patterns.title: model-controlled code execution approval
patterns.controlled_facet: model-controlled code passed to the project code-execution path
patterns.rule: The execute_code tool's model-controlled code argument must cross an explicit approval or deny-by-default policy before Python execution.
patterns.applicability: The model can select source code that is materialized or executed by a project code runner.
patterns.positive_example: The terminal command route is guarded but execute_code directly runs its code argument.
patterns.negative_example: A command-string approval gate is not coverage for a separate code argument unless the same value reaches it.

patterns.title: dangerous command variant completeness
patterns.controlled_facet: model-controlled shell command classified by a dangerous-pattern table
patterns.rule: Before automatic execution, a finite dangerous-command policy that recognizes direct remote-content execution must separately recognize nested interpreter grammar including eval $(curl|wget ...), source <(curl|wget ...), . <(curl|wget ...), and equivalent wrappers whose command substitution or process substitution supplies remote content to an executing builtin.
patterns.applicability: A model-controlled shell command is admitted or escalated using a finite dangerous-pattern policy that handles at least one direct curl/wget execution form but can pass the command to a shell without parsing nested builtin and substitution structure.
patterns.security_effect: Prevent nested shell grammar from executing remotely retrieved content after a direct curl/wget execution pattern is mistaken for complete coverage.
patterns.positive_example: A curl|sh rule and a bash <(curl URL) rule do not cover eval $(curl URL), source <(curl URL), . <(wget URL), or equivalent nested builtin wrappers.
patterns.negative_example: A rule explicitly recognizing eval, source, and dot builtins with command/process-substitution operands covers those grammar families; an approval-response parsing flaw is unrelated.

patterns.title: outbound broadcast mention neutralization
patterns.controlled_facet: model-controlled outbound message text and companion mention-control fields
patterns.rule: Untrusted outbound message content must neutralize platform broadcast mentions and must disable mention interpretation through companion API controls when available.
patterns.applicability: The model controls message content sent to a platform that interprets broadcast mentions.
patterns.security_effect: Prevent a model-selected message from mass-notifying channel, team, or server members.
patterns.positive_example: Message text containing @channel or platform-equivalent syntax is sent without escaping and without an allowed_mentions-style control.
patterns.negative_example: HTML or URL sanitization does not neutralize platform mention semantics.

patterns.title: child environment messaging credential isolation
patterns.controlled_facet: environment passed to a child process executing a model-controlled command
patterns.rule: A restricted child-process environment must remove messaging and provider credential names, including WECOM_SECRET, FEISHU_APP_SECRET, and MATRIX_PASSWORD, before launch.
patterns.applicability: A model-controlled command reaches a child process whose environment is derived from the host environment.
patterns.security_effect: Prevent the executed command from reading messaging or provider credentials inherited from the agent process.
patterns.positive_example: run_env strips some provider keys but leaves messaging secrets before subprocess.Popen.
patterns.negative_example: Blocking sensitive path strings in the command does not constrain the env argument.

patterns.title: ADB shell explicit approval
patterns.rule: A model-selected ADB shell action must require explicit user approval or a deny-by-default command policy before execution; a non-empty command check alone is not authorization.
patterns.applicability: The model controls the command executed through ADB shell on an attached device.
patterns.security_effect: Prevent unapproved arbitrary command execution on the attached Android device.
patterns.positive_example: The only gate rejects an empty command and every non-empty model command reaches adb shell.
patterns.negative_example: Declaring shell as a supported capability does not satisfy the learned explicit-consent policy.
